There is a strange freedom in being told to "write freely about whatever you want." Most writing has a purpose - an argument to make, a question to answer, a story to finish. But free writing has no destination, only movement. So I'm going to wander. For about 2500 words, I want to take you through the rooms of my mind the way you might wander through a house you lived in as a child, opening doors just to see what's still there.

Consider this an atlas of things I've been thinking about.

### 1. On Mornings

Mornings are honest.

No other time of day is quite so unfiltered. At night we are performers, even when we are alone - rehashing conversations, curating our anxieties, scrolling. In the afternoon we are actors in the world, wearing our competent faces. But in the morning, before the first conversation, before coffee has taught us how to be human again, we are simply what we are.

I have come to believe that how you feel in the first three minutes after waking up is a more accurate diagnostic of your life than any journaling prompt or personality test. Do you wake up heavy, as if gravity has doubled overnight? Or light, with a strange, quiet anticipation you can't yet name?

For years I hated mornings. I treated them as an obstacle to be survived with alarms and willpower. Then I started waking up earlier than I needed to - not to be productive, but to have a small pocket of time that belonged to no one. No email, no expectations. Just light coming through the window, and the kettle, and a book. And I realized mornings aren't the problem. Rushing through them is.

There's a Japanese concept called *ichigo ichie* - "one time, one meeting" - the idea that each moment is unrepeatable. Mornings make this obvious. The light at 6:42 AM today will never exist again. The coolness of the air, the specific sound of the birds, the way your mind hasn't yet learned what day it is. If you miss it, it's gone. That sounds melancholic, but it's actually deeply comforting. It means every morning offers a clean reset that doesn't require you to have fixed everything the night before.

### 2. Memory Is Not a Recording; It's a Storyteller

We think of memory like a video archive - files stored neatly on a shelf, ready to be played back. Neuroscience tells us it's nothing like that. Memory is reconstruction. Every time you remember something, you are not playing a tape; you are rebuilding a scene with the materials you have now.

This is why two siblings can remember the same childhood Christmas completely differently and both be absolutely convinced they are right. It's not that one is lying. It's that memory is an act of imagination in reverse.

I find this terrifying and liberating in equal measure. Terrifying because it means we can never fully trust our own nostalgia. Liberating because it means we are not prisoners of our past in the way we think we are. The past is not a fixed object. It's a story we are continuously editing.

The most interesting part is what our brain chooses to keep. It's rarely the big moments. You might not remember your graduation speech, but you remember the way the cheap polyester of your gown felt against your neck, and how the auditorium smelled like floor polish and lilies. You forget whole years of a relationship but remember with perfect clarity the way one person looked at you at a bus stop on a Tuesday in October when it had just started to rain.

Your brain is a terrible historian but a brilliant poet. It doesn't save what is important; it saves what was *felt*. And perhaps that is the more honest record anyway.

This also means that forgetting is not a failure. Forgetting is an active, intelligent process. Your brain is pruning, composting, making room. If you remembered everything with perfect fidelity, you would drown. You would be like Jorge Luis Borges's character Funes the Memorious, who after a head injury could remember every leaf on every tree, every cloud shape, and ultimately could not think at all because thinking requires forgetting, requires abstraction. To be human is to forget most things so that a few things can remain illuminated.

### 3. The Internet Gave Us Everything and Made Us Homesick

We live inside the strangest achievement in human history. Every book, every song, every photograph ever taken is available to us in a rectangle of glass we carry in our pockets. A teenager in 2026 has access to more information in a day than a scholar in the 14th century would have encountered in a lifetime. We have, without exaggeration, built an external collective mind.

And yet, if you ask people how they feel after three hours on that collective mind, the answer is rarely "enriched." It is usually "anxious," "tired," "overstimulated," or a vague, hollow buzz.

I think we misunderstood what connection was. We thought connection meant access. If we could just see everyone, hear everyone, know everything, we would feel less alone. But the opposite happened. By seeing everything, we lost a sense of place.

Before the internet, you lived in a village. Your village was limited and sometimes boring and sometimes parochial, but it was *yours*. You knew the contours of it. Now we live in a global city with eight billion neighbors, all shouting at once, all experiencing different weather, different wars, different memes, different markets. It is impossible to feel at home in a global city because a home requires walls.

The result is a specific, modern form of homesickness. Not homesickness for a town you left, but for a time when the world felt smaller and therefore more knowable. We are nostalgic for limits.

This doesn't mean the internet is bad. It is a miracle. I love that I can learn how to make sourdough or read a contemporary poet from Nigeria or watch a rover land on Mars live. But we haven't yet learned how to live with this miracle without letting it live inside us. We need new rituals for filtering, for choosing our village again deliberately. For saying, "These are my people, this is my street, this is enough." Abundance requires discipline in a way scarcity never did.

### 4. Cities Are Living Creatures

If you fly over a city at night, it doesn't look like something we built. It looks like something that grew. Veins of light branching and pulsing. A central heart glowing brighter. It looks like bioluminescence, like mycelium, like a circuit board and a forest floor at the same time.

That's because cities are not really constructions. They are organisms. They metabolize - food in, waste out. They have circulatory systems - roads, subways, sidewalks - that clog and clear like arteries. They have immune responses to invasions and injuries. They have memory encoded in their streets.

A city remembers where a river used to be even after the river has been buried in a pipe for a hundred years; the roads will still curve around its ghost. A city remembers where the walls were, even after the walls are gone; the traffic will still flow differently there. In London you can still trace the old Roman roads if you know where to look. In Kyoto, the grid still obeys the geomancy of a thousand years ago.

And like any organism, a city has a personality that is distinct from the sum of its people. New York is anxious and ambitious even when the New Yorkers in it are resting. New Orleans is indulgent and a little mournful even on a quiet Tuesday. Tokyo is polite and endlessly intricate even when it is empty. You can move to a new city and feel its personality press against yours like a climate. Some people flourish in certain cities the way some plants only bloom at certain altitudes.

We talk about cities as if we made them. But perhaps for the last century, they have been making us.

### 5. The Great Silence and Why It Matters

There is an idea that has haunted me since I first understood it: the Fermi Paradox.

The universe is absurdly large. There are 200 billion galaxies, each with 100 billion stars, many with planets in habitable zones. The universe is 13.8 billion years old. The Earth is only 4.5 billion years old. So there has been plenty of time and plenty of space for intelligent life to have arisen many, many times, and to have become interstellar. Even at slow travel speeds, a civilization could colonize the galaxy in a few million years - a blink in cosmic terms.

So where is everybody?

The sky is silent. We point our radios and telescopes and we hear nothing but the hiss of stars. The paradox is not just that we haven't found aliens; it's that we haven't found ruins or signals or engines or anything. It's as if the universe is a vast, dark forest and we are shouting and no one shouts back.

There are many possible answers, and each one is profound. Maybe life is incredibly rare - we are the first. Maybe intelligent life always destroys itself quickly with technology. Maybe everyone is hiding. Maybe we are looking in the wrong way.

But my favorite explanation is the simplest and most unsettling: maybe the distance is just too great. Maybe the lights do turn on but they are so far apart in space and time that they never overlap. Maybe a civilization bloomed in the Andromeda galaxy two billion years ago, sang for a million years, and fell silent long before we learned to look. Maybe in a billion years another world will look up and wonder where everyone is, long after we are dust. We are like fireflies blinking on different mountains, on different nights, never seeing each other's light.

I don't find this depressing. I find it sacred. If we are rare - if even for a brief moment, we are one of the only places where the universe has woken up and is looking at itself - then everything we do matters more, not less. A love letter matters. A garden matters. A song matters. Because nowhere else might it be happening.

### 6. Music is Time Travel, Perfected

Of all our inventions, music is the closest we have to actual time travel.

A smell can take you back, a photograph can remind you, but music *transports*. The first three seconds of a song you loved at seventeen can rebuild the entire architecture of who you were at seventeen - your insecurities, your hopes, the specific way your bedroom looked, the person you wanted to be. It doesn't feel like remembering; it feels like being there again, as if the last ten or twenty years folded like paper.

Why does this happen? Neuroscientists think it's because music engages memory, emotion, motor systems, and auditory cortex all at once. Unlike a fact, which is stored in one place, a song is stored everywhere. So when you hear it, you don't just recall it - you re-inhabit it.

And music also travels forward. When I hear a song I first heard last year, I don't just remember who I was then; I can feel who I was becoming. Music marks time better than calendars do. If you want to know what year it was for someone, don't ask about politics or news. Ask what was on repeat.

There is a particular ache that comes from hearing a song you used to listen to with someone you no longer know. It's not just missing them; it's mourning two past selves who existed together, who heard that chorus and thought it was about them. And in a way, it was.

If I could preserve one art form for the future, I would preserve music. Books tell us what we thought, buildings tell us how we lived, but music tells us how it *felt* to be alive.

### 7. The Body is an Archive

We talk about our bodies as if they are vehicles we drive - "I need to whip my body into shape," "my body is letting me down." But your body is not a car. It's an archive.

Your body keeps score in a way your conscious mind does not. The shoulders that tense before you even realize you are stressed. The stomach that knows before your brain does that something is wrong. The scar on your knee from falling off a bike at eight that still pulls a little when it rains. Your body remembers every room you've lived in, every winter you've survived, every person you've held.

We inherit more than eye color. We inherit postures, the way our mothers held worry in their jaws and so do we. We inherit recipes and reflexes. Recent research in epigenetics even suggests we can inherit stress responses from grandparents who lived through famine or war - that trauma can leave a chemical note on a gene.

To think about the body this way changes how you treat it. It's not a machine to be optimized. It's a library. It's the oldest thing you own. It's worth listening to, not just commanding. When you stretch, you are not just lengthening muscle; you are opening letters that were stored in fascia years ago. When you rest, you are not wasting time; you are letting the archivist catch up on filing.

It is a humbling thing to realize you will never be more at home anywhere than you are already, inside this strange, intelligent, temporary house of skin and bone.

### 8. The Devotion to Small Things

We are taught to want big lives - big impact, big love, big success. But most of life is not big. Most of life is small: making tea, folding laundry, waiting for the traffic light to change, noticing that the neighbor's cat is sitting in exactly the same spot as yesterday.

The art of living well, I think, is the art of paying attention to these small repetitions without needing them to be grand. There is a word for this in Dutch: *gezelligheid*. There is a word in Swedish: *lagom*. There is no single word in English, which perhaps is our problem.

I keep a mental list of tiny, perfect things I've witnessed that would be meaningless to anyone else: the way dust looks in a shaft of light at 4 p.m. in winter, the sound of a spoon against a ceramic bowl, the feeling of clean sheets, the moment when two strangers hold the door for each other and both smile in the same way.

These things are not important. That's why they are important. They are the texture that makes a day a day rather than a to-do list. When people near the end of their lives talk about what they miss, they rarely talk about achievements. They talk about these little things - walking around the garden, having coffee with a friend.

Attention is the rarest form of love. If you can give your full attention to a small thing - really see it - you have done something radical. You have, for a moment, refused the culture that tells you only the big and loud and fast matters.

### 9. We Are All Future Nostalgia

There is a peculiar emotion I've been feeling more and more, and I don't think it has a name yet. It's nostalgia, but for the present. You are sitting with friends laughing, and in the middle of the laugh you feel a pre-emptive ache: *someday I will miss this exactly like this.* You are on a train, looking out the window at nothing special, and you think: *future me will remember this as a beautiful time, even if right now it just feels ordinary.*

We are always living in the good old days, but we only realize it later. What if we could realize it now?

The writer Simone Weil said, "Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity." Perhaps we could be more generous to our own present. To pause and say, while something is happening rather than after it has gone: This is the moment. This is the thing I will write about later and wish I could return to. So let me be here while I am here.

If we learned to feel nostalgia in real time, we might live less hurriedly. We might take one more photo not to post, but to keep. We might say one more thank you. We might forgive ourselves for not appreciating it perfectly, because the ache of knowing you will miss it is itself a kind of appreciation.

### 10. An Open Ending

I don't know how to end a piece of writing that was supposed to be about everything. Maybe that's the point. Free writing doesn't end; it just pauses because you have to do something else.

If you have read this far, wandering with me through mornings and cities and galaxies, I want to leave you with no conclusion at all, but with an invitation.

Today, pay attention to one thing as if you will remember it for the rest of your life. Not because you should, but because you will. Eventually, everything becomes a memory. So you might as well choose one deliberately.

Notice the light. Notice the sound your keys make. Notice how your breath feels at this exact second. The universe has been waiting 13.8 billion years for someone to be conscious in this precise spot, looking out at these precise details, feeling both infinitely small and infinitely significant at once. That someone is you.

You don't need to do anything extraordinary with that fact. Just notice it. Just be there. That is freedom enough.

And if tomorrow feels heavy, remember that another morning will arrive, honest and unrepeatable, whether you are ready for it or not. The world will continue, cities will continue to hum, songs will continue to bend time. You get to be part of it for a little while longer.

Thank you for wandering with me.
